Aaron — thanks for the clear list and diagram. Quick summary up front, then a recommended checklist for netops below.

Short answer: we prefer customers configure stable egress IPs (SNAT or egress proxy) so you can IP allowlist our control-plane callbacks and diagnostic telemetry. We support both approaches but static egress IPs reduce operational friction.

High-level guidance:
- Outbound protocols: primarily HTTPS (443) to our control plane and model storage endpoints. No custom UDP ports required.
- Domains: we'll provide a minimal domain set (control API, telemetry, package repo). We also recommend allowing AWS S3 endpoints if you plan to use S3 for model hosting or backups; VPC endpoints are supported and preferred for full private traffic.
- Egress strategies supported:
  * Static NAT IPs (preferred) — allocate one or more Elastic NAT IPs and SNAT traffic from your subnets. Provide us the list for our allowlist.
  * Egress proxy — outbound connections via a corporate proxy with TLS pass-through. If TLS inspection is performed, ensure certs are compatible with our client cert exchange; we can provide our root if needed.
  * PrivateLink / VPC Endpoint — for fully private deployments of object stores or KMS, use VPC endpoints; note some telemetry will still route to the control plane unless you run the control plane in your VPC.

Checklist for netops (importable CSV attached: redwood-allowlist-template.csv):
1) Create outbound NAT with at least 2 static public IPs (for HA).
2) Configure SNAT so all inference/control traffic egresses from those IPs.
3) Allow outbound TCP 443 to the domain list we provide.
4) Allow DNS (UDP/TCP 53) to your resolvers — we rely on DNS to resolve model repo and control endpoints.
5) If you use VPC endpoints for S3/Secrets Manager, allow those endpoints in route table; otherwise allow S3 egress.
6) Open ports for NTP (udp 123) if your hosts need time sync to public NTP — preferably use internal NTP.
7) Add firewall rules for our IPs to your inbound control-plane firewall if you run the control plane in your VPC (we will give those IPs separately).
8) Add egress rules for telemetry endpoints and DocuSign/OSS downloads used during bootstrap.

Follow-ups: Dev will outline how the agent/client performs certificate pinning and where to put trusted roots; Marissa will propose a minimal IP/domain list by EOD tomorrow.

Aaron — adding technical detail on certificate handling and example ip/domains.

- Client TLS: our workload agent initiates outbound TLS to our control API. We support standard CA chains (no mutual TLS required for the public hosted model). If you run strict TLS inspection, you can either install our CA bundle on the inspection appliance or put the control-plane subnets behind the proxy bypass list.
- Certificate pinning: the agent pins our leaf certificates by SAN and issuer. If you terminate TLS at the proxy, ensure the proxy preserves SANs or we can provide a client-side option to disable pinning during install (not recommended).

Example minimal allowlist (we'll provide final list on Thursday):
- control.redwood.ai (443) — API calls and control-plane callbacks
- telemetry.redwood.ai (443) — heartbeat and anonymized metrics
- models.redwood-cdn.net (443) — model artifact downloads (we recommend VPC endpoint to S3 if you want no public egress)
- auth.redwood.ai (443) — token issuance

Notes on ephemeral scaling: when you autoscale inference pools we maintain the same SNAT IP range (if you use NAT gateway or our recommended SNAT instances). If you NAT individual worker nodes directly to ephemeral public IPs, you'll need to route through your static egress.

Attachment: redwood-allowlist-template.csv (CSV has columns: hostname, ip, port, description).

1) TLS termination at customer proxy: we can work with proxy-only egress. To avoid breaking pinning, two options:
